titleStmt.title: Inverted central auditory hierarchies for encoding local intervals and global temporal patterns
titleStmt.author: Asokan
Williamson
Hancock
Polley

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Inverted central auditory hierarchies for encoding local intervals and global temporal patterns

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how the timescale of neural activity changes from midbrain to cortex, and what each stage can therefore encode
span.quote: Here, we addressed whether low-level auditory neurons with fast timescales encode brief local features of sounds but not the longer gestalt, while the slower neural timescales in higher-level auditory areas may support the encoding of global sound patterns organized over longer time scales

span.label: whether the slow timescales that cost the cortex temporal precision are what let it encode global patterns that subcortical stations cannot
span.quote: While the slow neural timescales in the cortex may interfere with precise temporal coding, we reasoned that the sluggish temporal processing could suggest a cortical advantage over subcortical stations for encoding slowly evolving features.

span.label: shows the auditory hierarchy is inverted between two encoding jobs - fidelity for local intervals falls from IC to A1 while sensitivity to global rhythm appears only in A1 - and that the cortical signal is carried by spike timing with no change in firing rate
span.quote: Asokan et al. show an emergent sensitivity for slow temporal rhythms at the level of the auditory cortex. Whereas single units in the mouse midbrain and thalamus encode local temporal intervals with high fidelity, cortical units integrate over extended periods to distinguish between random or regular interval sequences by adjusting spike timing.

span.label: existence
span.quote: These findings show that low-level auditory neurons with fast timescales encode isolated sound features but not the longer gestalt, while the extended timescales in higher-level areas can facilitate sensitivity to slower contextual changes in the sensory environment.

span.label: hierarchical temporal coding in the central auditory pathway
span.quote: We performed simultaneous single unit ensemble recordings from three hierarchical stages of auditory processing in awake mice – the inferior colliculus (IC), medial geniculate body of the thalamus (MGB) and primary auditory cortex (A1).

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: To test this idea, we used three high-density probes to make simultaneous recordings from hundreds of single units along the IC-MGB-A1 hierarchy in awake, head-fixed mice ( Figure 1B ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Dendrite-targeting cortical GABAergic interneurons dampen pyramidal-neuron spike decay when stimulus timing becomes predictable
span.quote: Cortical GABAergic neurons that express somatostatin or neuron-derived neurotrophic factor are clear candidates to dampen principal neuron spiking timing because they target the distal dendrites of A1 pyramidal neurons to regulate network excitability and recurrent excitation, but are also sensitive to slowly changing internal state variables.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Corticothalamic feedback recruits thalamic reticular nucleus inhibition, which dampens feedforward thalamocortical drive during rhythms
span.quote: These effects hint at an additional (or alternative) circuit mediated through corticothalamic feedback, which could dampen feedforward thalamocortical synaptic inputs via inhibition from the thalamic reticular nucleus.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Cortex switches from a recurrent deliberative mode to a pass-through mode once incoming sound matches internal predictive models
span.quote: This may reflect a physiological transition in the cortex from a “deliberative” mode when sound features are unpredictable, typified by strong inter- and intra-columnar recurrent activity, to a “pass through” mode when environmental stimuli match internal predictive models.

span.label: the cortex reads regularity by compressing its own spike decay constant, not by changing how much it fires
span.quote: Intriguingly, it was the neural timescale itself that conveyed whether the noise bursts were arranged randomly or in a rhythm; A1 spiking decayed more rapidly when the time intervals fell into a predictable rhythm than when they were arranged in a random sequence.

span.label: the timescale that changes is about 40x faster than the stimulus feature driving it, so the sensitivity must be inherited from other circuits rather than computed by the unit itself
span.quote: It is interesting that cortical spiking timescales are sensitive to a stimulus feature that is approximately 40× slower than the timescale itself (800ms vs 20ms), which suggests that A1 regular-spiking unit timescale dynamics are likely the product of other local or long-range circuits that respond more directly to the change in predicable stimulus timing.

span.label: candidate source: dendrite-targeting somatostatin or NDNF interneurons that dampen recurrent excitation and track slow state variables
span.quote: Cortical GABAergic neurons that express somatostatin or neuron-derived neurotrophic factor are clear candidates to dampen principal neuron spiking timing because they target the distal dendrites of A1 pyramidal neurons to regulate network excitability and recurrent excitation, but are also sensitive to slowly changing internal state variables.

span.label: alternative source: corticothalamic feedback damping thalamocortical input through the thalamic reticular nucleus, suggested by the weaker MGB effect
span.quote: On the other hand, a subset of thalamic units also showed strong modulation of neural timescales and reduced firing rates during rhythmic contexts. These effects hint at an additional (or alternative) circuit mediated through corticothalamic feedback, which could dampen feedforward thalamocortical synaptic inputs via inhibition from the thalamic reticular nucleus.

span.label: stimulus-specific adaptation, the nearest neighbouring phenomenon, works instead by synaptic fatigue for standard inputs while deviant inputs stay unadapted
span.quote: As the name implies, SSA is fundamentally a spike rate adaptation process dominated by synaptic fatigue for standard inputs, whereas synaptic inputs elicited by improbable deviant inputs remain unadapted, or even potentiated through as yet undefined recurrent or descending circuit mechanisms.

span.label: peripheral speed is a design constraint: the morphologies and synapses that give the early stages sub-millisecond precision are what make them unsuited to slow structure
span.quote: Each of these remarkable feats of high-speed processing are enabled by cellular morphologies, intrinsic electrical properties and synaptic architectures that are unique to the first stages of auditory processing and are indispensable for encoding the rapid acoustic building blocks of sound perception.

span.label: Cortical sensitivity to regularity did not extend to longer or more complex cycles, so the integration window demonstrated is bounded at roughly 0.8-1.6 s.
span.note: what this limits: the regularity result, with its ceiling measured: SINGLE UNIT SENSITIVITY TO REGULARITY IS LIMITED TO STIMULUS TIMESCALES ON THE ORDER OF 4-8 REPEATING ELEMENTS OR 0.8-1.6s
span.quote: Therefore, at least for A1 in passively listening mice, single unit sensitivity to regularity is limited to stimulus timescales on the order of 4-8 repeating elements or 0.8 – 1.6s.

span.label: Only A1 in passively listening mice was studied; higher-order fields and behaviourally engaged listening remain to be tested.
span.note: what this limits: the generality beyond A1 and beyond passive listening: it would be important to test the CANDIDATE HIGHER-ORDER AREAS ... PARTICULARLY WHEN MICE ARE BEHAVIORALLY ENGAGED
span.quote: In future work, it would be important to test whether even more protracted spiking timescales and more integrative processing of slower developing regularities are encoded in candidate higher-order areas of the mouse auditory cortex, such as the dorsal-posterior and ventral-posterior fields, particularly when mice are behaviorally engaged in active listening tasks.

span.label: The circuit that actually confers sensitivity to the ~800 ms regularity is not identified; candidate local and long-range mechanisms are only conjectured.
span.note: what this limits: any mechanistic reading: the timescale dynamics ARE LIKELY THE PRODUCT OF OTHER LOCAL OR LONG-RANGE CIRCUITS THAT RESPOND MORE DIRECTLY TO THE CHANGE IN PREDICTABILITY - the circuit that confers the sensitivity is not identified
span.quote: It is interesting that cortical spiking timescales are sensitive to a stimulus feature that is approximately 40× slower than the timescale itself (800ms vs 20ms), which suggests that A1 regular-spiking unit timescale dynamics are likely the product of other local or long-range circuits that respond more directly to the change in predicable stimulus timing.

span.label: the cortical sensitivity has a measured ceiling - it holds for cycles of four to eight intervals and is gone at twelve
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 0 - the effect holds for cycles of four to eight and is gone beyond
span.quote: Therefore, at least for A1 in passively listening mice, single unit sensitivity to regularity is limited to stimulus timescales on the order of 4-8 repeating elements or 0.8 – 1.6s.

span.label: passive listening only; whether engagement in a task extends the integration window is untested
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 1, for engagement specifically - only passive listening was tested
span.quote: In future work, it would be important to test whether even more protracted spiking timescales and more integrative processing of slower developing regularities are encoded in candidate higher-order areas of the mouse auditory cortex, such as the dorsal-posterior and ventral-posterior fields, particularly when mice are behaviorally engaged in active listening tasks.

span.label: only A1 was recorded, so the higher-order fields where longer regularities might be encoded were not sampled
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 1, for anatomy specifically - only A1 was recorded, so the higher-order fields where longer regularities might be encoded were not sampled
span.quote: In future work, it would be important to test whether even more protracted spiking timescales and more integrative processing of slower developing regularities are encoded in candidate higher-order areas of the mouse auditory cortex, such as the dorsal-posterior and ventral-posterior fields, particularly when mice are behaviorally engaged in active listening tasks.

span.label: cell class is inferred from spike waveform width, not from a molecular marker
span.note: what this limits: every result reported by cell class: REGULAR and FAST SPIKING are assigned by THE TROUGH TO PEAK INTERVAL ... EXCEEDING 0.6ms, a waveform proxy rather than a molecular identification
span.quote: For the regular versus fast spike waveform classification, the trough to peak interval of the mean spike waveform formed a bimodal distribution, which was used to subdivide neurons with intervals exceeding 0.6ms as regular spiking, while neurons with intervals shorter than 0.6ms were fast spiking

span.label: the neural-timescale metric (decay constant of an exponential fit to the spike-count autocorrelation), developed for hierarchies of visual cortical areas and here applied to the auditory pathway
span.quote: Neural timescales also increase across hierarchies of visual cortical areas, where it is quantified as the decay time constant ( τ ) of an exponential fit to the temporal spike count autocorrelation.

span.label: the autocorrelation-decay measure of neural timescale, and the expectation that it lengthens up a hierarchy
span.quote: Neural timescales also increase across hierarchies of visual cortical areas, where it is quantified as the decay time constant ( τ ) of an exponential fit to the temporal spike count autocorrelation.

span.label: the paradigm of contrasting repeating with random acoustic patterns
span.quote: The protocol we introduce here was inspired by changes in cortical activity and perceptual awareness of complex repeating acoustic patterns in human subjects.

span.label: the binary support vector machine, used here as a readout of ensemble state
span.quote: We then used a binary support vector machine (SVM) on the principal components projection to classify whether ensemble activity for each cycle came from the rhythmic or random stimulus context

span.label: a random-random stimulus, keeping the stimulus random for all 50 post-baseline cycles instead of switching from rhythmic to random (Figure S4 - three sentences describe this one control, recorded once)
span.quote: To control for the possibility that the ordinal arrangement of random following rhythmic could account for differences in spike patterning, we created a random-random stimulus but found that classification was near chance throughout and no systematic changes in neural timescales were observed ( Figure S4 ).

span.label: repeating the whole analysis on cycle-order-shuffled data, for every recording in all three brain regions - the exclusion is carried by the word shuffling rather than spelled out, hence the lower weight
span.quote: As a control, we performed the same analysis after shuffling the ordering of cycles and we repeat this process for each recording in all three brain regions.

span.label: neural timescale = the decay constant of a single unit's spike-count autocorrelation, about 20ms in A1 - NOT the window over which the unit integrates, which is 800ms; the paper states the 40x gap itself
span.quote: It is interesting that cortical spiking timescales are sensitive to a stimulus feature that is approximately 40× slower than the timescale itself (800ms vs 20ms), which suggests that A1 regular-spiking unit timescale dynamics are likely the product of other local or long-range circuits that respond more directly to the change in predicable stimulus timing.

span.label: regular, sense 1 = a property of the stimulus sequence (intervals repeating in a fixed order), the paper's independent variable
span.quote: First, with the protocol described here, there are no low- or high-probability stimuli. All stimuli were identical frozen noise bursts separated by a single set of intervals used in both random and regular contexts. The only explicit feature that distinguished random from regular contexts was whether the sequence of inter-burst intervals repeated across cycles or randomly arranged from one cycle to the next.

span.label: regular, sense 2 = a waveform class of neuron (trough-to-peak > 0.6ms, putative pyramidal); same word, unrelated referent, both used throughout
span.quote: For the regular versus fast spike waveform classification, the trough to peak interval of the mean spike waveform formed a bimodal distribution, which was used to subdivide neurons with intervals exceeding 0.6ms as regular spiking, while neurons with intervals shorter than 0.6ms were fast spiking

span.label: context = the global statistics of the stimulus sequence (random vs rhythmic), not behavioural or task context
span.quote: Like the protocol we used here, SSA is characterized by contrasting the neural response to an identical stimulus that differs only according to global context.

span.label: tonotopy here is an instrument, not an object: the frequency gradient and its reversal are used to certify that the probe is in A1
span.quote: We ensured recordings were made from A1 based on the best frequency gradient along the rostro-caudal axis and the tonotopic reversal towards the rostral edge of the craniotomy.

span.label: hierarchy = the ascending anatomical pathway IC to MGB to A1, ordered by synaptic distance from the cochlea
span.quote: Neural timescales significantly increased across the hierarchy (Kruskal-Wallis, 1.7x10 −10 ; post-hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, IC vs MGB, 1/0.05; IC vs A1, 1x10 −6 /0.51; MGB vs A1, 1x10 −8 /0.41 for p-value/Cliff’s delta).

span.label: claim_type: existence
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: existence — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: We observed that the changes in ensemble spiking were sufficient to classify the change from rhythmic to random sequences in A1, but not in MGB or IC

span.label: method: simultaneous three-probe extracellular single-unit recording from IC, MGB and A1 of awake head-fixed mice, with template-matching interval decoding and an SVM on principal components of ensemble spiking
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: electrophysiology — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: To test this idea, we used three high-density probes to make simultaneous recordings from hundreds of single units along the IC-MGB-A1 hierarchy in awake, head-fixed mice

span.label: phenomenon: emergent cortical sensitivity to the regularity of a sequence of intervals, expressed as compression of the spike decay constant
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: hierarchical temporal coding in the central auditory pathway — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Intriguingly, it was the neural timescale itself that conveyed whether the noise bursts were arranged randomly or in a rhythm; A1 spiking decayed more rapidly when the time intervals fell into a predictable rhythm than when they were arranged in a random sequence.

span.label: replicates → previously documented progressive loss of temporal fidelity along the ascending auditory pathway (reviews cited as refs 1, 2, 4)
span.quote: From midbrain to cortex, decoding accuracy was reduced overall and restricted to a limited range of longer intervals ( Figure 1G ), such that the median threshold of interval decoding rose from 1.4ms for IC units, to 16ms for MGB units, and 64ms in A1 ( Figure 1H ), reflecting a progressive loss of temporal fidelity along the ascending auditory pathway that has been documented in many previous studies (for reviews see 1 , 2 , 4 ).

span.label: extends → prior animal work on stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA) and contrast gain control (refs 17, 20-26)
span.quote: While our approach is conceptually similar to prior work on SSA or contrast gain control in animal models, the methodological approach and neurophysiological results differ in several key respects.

span.label: builds-on → the neural-timescale measure (autocorrelation decay constant) established across visual cortical hierarchies (refs 6, 7)
span.quote: Adapting this approach to our data, we confirmed a progression of neural timescales in the auditory system that approximately doubled from midbrain to cortex ( Figure 1D ).

span.label: builds-on → human work on cortical activity and perceptual awareness of complex repeating acoustic patterns (refs 15, 16)
span.quote: The protocol we introduce here was inspired by changes in cortical activity and perceptual awareness of complex repeating acoustic patterns in human subjects.

span.label: distinguishes-from → stimulus-specific adaptation and contrast gain control
span.quote: While our approach is conceptually similar to prior work on SSA or contrast gain control in animal models, the methodological approach and neurophysiological results differ in several key respects.

span.label: distinguishes-from → SSA and contrast gain control, on anatomical distribution
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS ANATOMICAL DISTRIBUTION. 'while SSA, contrast gain control or other neural signatures of stimulus context changes are robustly expressed in the A1, THEY ARE ALSO CLEARLY REPRESENTED THE IC AND MGB. The context sensitivity we report here is COMPLETELY ABSENT IN OUR SAMPLE OF IC UNITS.' The known adaptation phenomena appear at every level; this one does not - so a cortical result that resembles them is distinguished by WHERE ELSE IT CAN BE FOUND rather than by what it looks like. Q-495.
span.quote: Third, while SSA, 20 - 22 contrast gain control, 23 - 25 or other neural signatures of stimulus context changes 26 are robustly expressed in the A1, they are also clearly represented the IC and MGB. The context sensitivity we report here is completely absent in our sample of IC units and is weakly expressed in MGB neurons.

span.label: distinguishes-from → rate-based accounts of context-dependent adaptation
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS WHAT CARRIES THE SIGNAL - RATE OR TEMPORAL PATTERN. 'SSA, CONTRAST GAIN CONTROL AND OTHER FORMS OF CONTEXT-DEPENDENT ADAPTATION ARE BASED ON CHANGES IN SPIKE RATE, WHEREAS our findings demonstrate that RANDOM OR RHYTHMIC ARRANGEMENTS OF TEMPORAL INTERVALS CAN BE DECODED FROM A1 SPIKING.' The existing accounts are not denied their data; they are denied coverage of a signal their measure cannot see. Q-494.
span.quote: Fourth, and perhaps most importantly, SSA, contrast gain control and other forms of context-dependent adaptation are based on changes in spike rate, whereas our findings demonstrate that random or rhythmic arrangements of temporal intervals can be decoded from A1 spiking ( Figure 2D ) without any change in mean spike rate ( Figure 3E - F ). Instead, stimulus context was represented solely by changes in how sound-evoked spikes were arranged in time.

span.label: extends → human work on cortical responses to repeating acoustic patterns
span.quote: The protocol we introduce here was inspired by changes in cortical activity and perceptual awareness of complex repeating acoustic patterns in human subjects.

span.label: builds-on → visual-cortex measurements of neural timescale by autocorrelation decay
span.quote: Neural timescales also increase across hierarchies of visual cortical areas, where it is quantified as the decay time constant ( τ ) of an exponential fit to the temporal spike count autocorrelation.

span.label: confirms → prior reports of declining temporal fidelity along the ascending auditory pathway
span.quote: From midbrain to cortex, decoding accuracy was reduced overall and restricted to a limited range of longer intervals ( Figure 1G ), such that the median threshold of interval decoding rose from 1.4ms for IC units, to 16ms for MGB units, and 64ms in A1 ( Figure 1H ), reflecting a progressive loss of temporal fidelity along the ascending auditory pathway that has been documented in many previous studies

span.label: neural timescale —operationalised-as→ decay time constant
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — imported from visual-cortex hierarchy work; the quote names the source field as well as the measure
span.quote: Neural timescales also increase across hierarchies of visual cortical areas, where it is quantified as the decay time constant ( τ ) of an exponential fit to the temporal spike count autocorrelation.

span.label: stimulus regularity —operationalised-as→ inter-burst intervals repeated across cycles
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: First, with the protocol described here, there are no low- or high-probability stimuli. All stimuli were identical frozen noise bursts separated by a single set of intervals used in both random and regular contexts. The only explicit feature that distinguished random from regular contexts was whether the sequence of inter-burst intervals repeated across cycles or randomly arranged from one cycle to the next.

span.label: A1 —operationalised-as→ best frequency gradient
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — tonotopy as the criterion for having reached A1 - the same word is the object of study elsewhere in this corpus
span.quote: We ensured recordings were made from A1 based on the best frequency gradient along the rostro-caudal axis and the tonotopic reversal towards the rostral edge of the craniotomy.

span.label: regular spiking —operationalised-as→ trough to peak interval
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — cut at 0.6ms; fast spiking is the same measure on the other side of it
span.quote: For the regular versus fast spike waveform classification, the trough to peak interval of the mean spike waveform formed a bimodal distribution, which was used to subdivide neurons with intervals exceeding 0.6ms as regular spiking, while neurons with intervals shorter than 0.6ms were fast spiking

span.label: fast spiking —same-as→ putative parvalbumin-expressing interneuron
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.6 — the record marks this weak — an identity asserted by apposition and hedged by 'putative'; the evidence for it is waveform width, not a marker
span.quote: Neural timescales were equivalently compressed for regular spiking putative pyramidal neurons across A1 layers ( Figure S2 ), yet no effect of context was observed in fast spiking putative parvalbumin-expressing interneurons

span.label: context sensitivity —distinct-from→ SSA
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — discriminated by anatomical distribution: SSA is expressed in IC and MGB too, this is absent in IC
span.quote: Third, while SSA, 20 - 22 contrast gain control, 23 - 25 or other neural signatures of stimulus context changes 26 are robustly expressed in the A1, they are also clearly represented the IC and MGB. The context sensitivity we report here is completely absent in our sample of IC units and is weakly expressed in MGB neurons.

span.label: context sensitivity —distinct-from→ contrast gain control
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — same demarcation paragraph; its fourth point, rate versus timing, is carried in claim_relations
span.quote: Third, while SSA, 20 - 22 contrast gain control, 23 - 25 or other neural signatures of stimulus context changes 26 are robustly expressed in the A1, they are also clearly represented the IC and MGB. The context sensitivity we report here is completely absent in our sample of IC units and is weakly expressed in MGB neurons.

span.label: SSA —is-a→ spike rate adaptation
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: As the name implies, SSA is fundamentally a spike rate adaptation process dominated by synaptic fatigue for standard inputs, whereas synaptic inputs elicited by improbable deviant inputs remain unadapted, or even potentiated through as yet undefined recurrent or descending circuit mechanisms.

span.label: decay constant —distinct-from→ mean firing rate
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — dissociated empirically in the same units and the same 100ms window, not merely conceptually
span.quote: Presenting the intervals in rhythmic patterns had no consistent effect on mean firing rate within the 100ms response window ( Figure 3E - F ), but instead only on how the spikes were arranged withing the 100ms response window, both in terms of shorter decay constants and less variation in first spike latency

span.label: A1 —contrasted-with→ IC
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — on rhythm classification the cortex succeeds and the midbrain fails - the reverse of the interval-decoding ordering
span.quote: We observed that the changes in ensemble spiking were sufficient to classify the change from rhythmic to random sequences in A1, but not in MGB or IC

span.label: A1 —contrasted-with→ MGB
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: We observed that the changes in ensemble spiking were sufficient to classify the change from rhythmic to random sequences in A1, but not in MGB or IC

span.label: slow neural timescales —causes→ interfere with precise temporal coding
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — the cost. Same property and same sentence as the edge below, opposite valence - the sign lives in the target, not in a note
span.quote: While the slow neural timescales in the cortex may interfere with precise temporal coding, we reasoned that the sluggish temporal processing could suggest a cortical advantage over subcortical stations for encoding slowly evolving features.

span.label: slow neural timescales —causes→ cortical advantage
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — the capability: an advantage over subcortical stations for encoding slowly evolving features
span.quote: While the slow neural timescales in the cortex may interfere with precise temporal coding, we reasoned that the sluggish temporal processing could suggest a cortical advantage over subcortical stations for encoding slowly evolving features.

span.label: rhythmic patterns —causes→ shorter decay constants
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — the headline effect, stated in the same sentence that rules out any change in mean firing rate
span.quote: Presenting the intervals in rhythmic patterns had no consistent effect on mean firing rate within the 100ms response window ( Figure 3E - F ), but instead only on how the spikes were arranged withing the 100ms response window, both in terms of shorter decay constants and less variation in first spike latency

span.label: A1 —part-of→ IC-MGB-A1 hierarchy
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Classification accuracy increases along the IC-MGB-A1 hierarchy (Two-way repeated measures ANOVAs, main effect for classification over cycles: IC [F = 0.5, p = 0.99], MGB [F = 0.69, p = 0.93], A1 [F = 18.81, p = 0]; interaction term for classification × condition, IC [F = 1.23, p = 0.15], MGB [F = 1.55, p = 0.01], A1, [F = 21.28, p = 0]).

span.label: IC —part-of→ ascending auditory pathway
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: From midbrain to cortex, decoding accuracy was reduced overall and restricted to a limited range of longer intervals ( Figure 1G ), such that the median threshold of interval decoding rose from 1.4ms for IC units, to 16ms for MGB units, and 64ms in A1 ( Figure 1H ), reflecting a progressive loss of temporal fidelity along the ascending auditory pathway that has been documented in many previous studies

span.label: Kruskal-Wallis test
span.quote: Neural timescales significantly increased across the hierarchy (Kruskal-Wallis, 1.7x10 −10 ; post-hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, IC vs MGB, 1/0.05; IC vs A1, 1x10 −6 /0.51; MGB vs A1, 1x10 −8 /0.41 for p-value/Cliff’s delta).

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: Interval classification accuracy is significantly reduced at successive stages of the IC-MGB-A1 hierarchy (Mixed design ANOVA, main effect for structure, F = 20.95, p = 6x10 −9 ).

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: Classification accuracy increases along the IC-MGB-A1 hierarchy (Two-way repeated measures ANOVAs, main effect for classification over cycles: IC [F = 0.5, p = 0.99], MGB [F = 0.69, p = 0.93], A1 [F = 18.81, p = 0]

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Asterisk denotes statistical significance with a paired t-test (p < 0.05 and Cohen’s d > 0.5); (IC, 0.7/0.05; MGB, 0.00009/0.33; A1, 3x10 −14 /0.65 for p-value/Cohen’s d).

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Neural timescales are significantly reduced during rhythmic epochs in A1, slightly reduced in the MGB, but not affected in the IC (one-sample t-test against a population mean of 0; IC, 0.27/0.08; MGB, 0.00002/0.33; A1, 8x10 −13 /0.59 for p-value/Cohen’s d).

span.label: effect size
span.quote: Effect sizes were estimated with Cohen’s d for normally distributed data and with Cliff’s delta for samples that did not conform to a normal distribution.

span.label: normality test
span.quote: The Lilliefors test was used to check for normality of the data.

span.label: multiple-comparison correction
span.quote: Multiple post-hoc comparisons were corrected using Bonferroni correction.

span.label: principal component analysis
span.quote: From the simultaneously recorded ensemble of neurons within each region, we reduced dimensionality using principal component analysis.

span.label: support vector machine classification
span.quote: We then fed the responses from the top principal components that capture 75% the variance in the data to a SVM with a linear kernel.

span.label: cross-validation
span.quote: We trained and cross-validated the classifier using 10-fold cross-validation which was iterated 100 times with a different random split for each iteration.

span.label: Kruskal-Wallis
span.quote: Neural timescales significantly increased across the hierarchy (Kruskal-Wallis, 1.7x10 −10 ; post-hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, IC vs MGB, 1/0.05; IC vs A1, 1x10 −6 /0.51; MGB vs A1, 1x10 −8 /0.41 for p-value/Cliff’s delta).

span.label: Cliff's delta
span.quote: Neural timescales significantly increased across the hierarchy (Kruskal-Wallis, 1.7x10 −10 ; post-hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, IC vs MGB, 1/0.05; IC vs A1, 1x10 −6 /0.51; MGB vs A1, 1x10 −8 /0.41 for p-value/Cliff’s delta).

span.label: Bonferroni correction
span.quote: Neural timescales significantly increased across the hierarchy (Kruskal-Wallis, 1.7x10 −10 ; post-hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, IC vs MGB, 1/0.05; IC vs A1, 1x10 −6 /0.51; MGB vs A1, 1x10 −8 /0.41 for p-value/Cliff’s delta).

span.label: one-sample t-test
span.quote: Neural timescales are significantly reduced when noise bursts form rhythms than during random arrangements with cycle sizes of 4, but not 8 or 12 (one-sample t-test against a population mean of 0, 4 intervals, 2x10 −12 /0.59; 8 intervals, 0.002/0.24; 12 intervals, 0.31/0.08, for p-value/Cohen’s d).

span.label: Cohen's d
span.quote: Neural timescales are significantly reduced when noise bursts form rhythms than during random arrangements with cycle sizes of 4, but not 8 or 12 (one-sample t-test against a population mean of 0, 4 intervals, 2x10 −12 /0.59; 8 intervals, 0.002/0.24; 12 intervals, 0.31/0.08, for p-value/Cohen’s d).

span.label: two-way repeated measures ANOVA
span.quote: Classification accuracy increases along the IC-MGB-A1 hierarchy (Two-way repeated measures ANOVAs, main effect for classification over cycles: IC [F = 0.5, p = 0.99], MGB [F = 0.69, p = 0.93], A1 [F = 18.81, p = 0]; interaction term for classification × condition, IC [F = 1.23, p = 0.15], MGB [F = 1.55, p = 0.01], A1, [F = 21.28, p = 0]).
